comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Root cause found, and it is upstream of the symmetric-memory design question this issue opens with. The two aliasing windows come from one scalar: the step counter's sharding.

`_init_state` is `@jax.jit` with no explicit `out_shardings` (`experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py:1006`), so `step=jnp.array(0, dtype=jnp.int32)` (`:763`) comes back under a `GSPMDSharding({replicated})`. `train_step` runs under the explicit mesh and returns `step=state.step + one` (`:933`) under a `NamedSharding`. JAX keys its compilation cache on input shardings, so the second step misses the cache and compiles a second executable, which then serves the rest of the run while the first stays alive in the cache. Every other state leaf already carries an explicit sharding and matches across the step.

`CollectiveMemoryCache` is a member of `GpuExecutable`, so two executables means two `ncclCommWindowRegister` calls over the same collective-memory arena, at the same base address, with identical size. NCCL 2.30.7 accepts the duplicate: commit `52f6d00` deleted the backing-allocation dedup loop from `symMemoryObtain`, which is present at `src/dev_runtime.cc:615` in `v2.30.4-1` and gone in `v2.30.7-1`. Nothing in the registration path checks for overlap.

The failure then comes from the lookup. `ncclDevrFindWindow` (`src/dev_runtime.cc:1401`) resolves an address to the **last** window registered there, so the eval's 518,436,864-byte window shadows the two 20,293,761,024-byte train windows at `0xbf80000000`. An access at an offset past the smaller window's size fails `ncclDevrGetLsaRankPtr`'s `offset >= winHost->size` test, which returns a bare `ncclInvalidArgument` with no WARN. That is why `NCCL_DEBUG=WARN` produces nothing and XLA itself reports `Last NCCL warning(error) log entry ''`.

Measured on one rack at d6144 (48 layers, EP64, `--watch-mode inline`, no evaluator): 128 `jit(train_step)` XLA compilations and 128 registrations of `ptr=0xbf80000000; size=20293761024` across 64 ranks, two of each per rank. The same run at 12 layers gives 64 and 64. A per-leaf `Format` diff across one step names exactly one drifting leaf: `.step`, `GSPMDSharding({replicated}, memory_kind=device)` before and `NamedSharding(mesh=Mesh('replica_dcn':1,'data':1,'expert':64,'model':1), ...)` after. It is not a tracing retrace — `JAX_EXPLAIN_CACHE_MISSES=1` reports only "never seen function" for inner functions and never for `train_step`.

Two avenues are closed. NCCL 2.31.2 does not fix this: `ra2a-8870-nccl2312-r2` ran `NCCL version 2.31.2+cuda13.3`, completed a train step and both evals, then failed character-identically to its 2.30.7 sibling `ra2a-evalnccl-c13d1` at the eval-to-train handoff on 42 of 64 ranks. NCCL's fix (`8b6b8b6`/`5a4b7fa`) is on `origin/dev` and `origin/staging` and in no tag. Upstream XLA has no fix either: `collective_memory*.{cc,h}` and `nccl_symmetric_memory.*` are byte-identical between the pinned base `dcf304bc5d` and `upstream/main`.

#8859 removed the third executable, not the aliasing. Two windows per rank are registered in every d6144 ragged run, including both that hung in #8870.

Fix: place the step counter on the sharding the train step returns it with, once the state is finalised. One executable, one window, and this collision becomes impossible rather than avoided by keeping the capacity-limited evaluator off. Note `jax.device_put` is not usable here — it asserts inside `_different_device_order_reshard` when the source is a `GSPMDSharding` whose device order differs from the mesh's — so the reshard goes through a small `jit` with `out_shardings`. The change is committed on `mcwitt/8870-repro`; verification at the hero shape is running and should show 64 compilations and 64 registrations.

One caveat for whoever reviews this: the depth dependence is unexplained. The same sharding mismatch should exist at 12 layers, yet a 12-layer run registers one window. The fix does not depend on resolving that, but the small-scale case should not be assumed to be understood.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Fix verified at the hero shape on one rack. The run completed with 64 `jit(train_step)` XLA compilations and 64 registrations of `ptr=0xbf80000000; size=20293761024` across 64 ranks, one of each per rank, against 128 and 128 before the change. The per-leaf `Format` diff across a step now reports `identical across the step`, so the drift is gone rather than only its effect.

Configuration was d6144, 48 layers, EP64 on one NVL72 rack, `--moe-implementation ragged_all_to_all --master-params device --watch-mode inline --watch-interval 10`, no evaluator, counted with `TF_CPP_MIN_LOG_LEVEL=0 TF_CPP_VMODULE=nccl_symmetric_memory=3` and `JAX_LOG_COMPILES=1`.

One implementation note for review: `jax.device_put` cannot be used to place the counter, because it hits an assertion inside JAX's `_different_device_order_reshard` when the source is a `GSPMDSharding` whose device order differs from the mesh's. The reshard goes through a small `jit` with `out_shardings` instead, which costs nothing for a scalar.

With one executable there is one symmetric window per rank, so a second executable of any footprint can no longer shadow it, and the capacity-limited evaluator can be re-enabled once this lands. That is the condition this issue asks for, reached from the JAX side rather than by changing how XLA registers the arena.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 The aliasing is now confirmed directly at the hero's own scale, which the earlier one-rack measurements could only imply. An eleven-rack run on 2026-09-03 at the hero shape, restored from `step-54000` with the step-counter fix deliberately switched off, registered **1408 arena windows across 704 ranks — exactly two per rank** — of size 20,293,761,024 at the same base, alongside 1408 `jit_train_step` compilations and 16,896 of the 2 MiB per-thunk barrier-signal windows. That is the two-executables-one-arena condition this issue describes, observed at 704 ranks rather than 64.

The fix holds the other way at the same scale: with the step counter placed on the mesh the train step returns it with, the count is one executable and one arena window per rank.

Also worth recording here, because it bears on the symmetric-memory design question this issue opens with: the pinned PJRT wheel compiles its device kernels against `HERMETIC_NCCL_VERSION="2.29.7"` (`tensorflow.bazelrc:192`) while the runtime resolves to 2.30.7. NCCL's `ncclDevCommCompat_v22907` shim forces `ginType = NONE` and gates `deviceApiSupport` on the clique being a single LSA team. The relevant consequence for this issue is that the deployed kernel is built without 2.30's system-scope release fence in the barrier's `arrive`, and that `52f6d00` — which removed the backing-registration dedup from `symMemoryObtain` and is what lets two identical registrations over one allocation both succeed — shipped *in* 2.30.7, i.e. in the runtime we use but not in the headers we compile against. The upstream restoration (`8b6b8b6`/`5a4b7fa`, on `origin/dev`, in no tag) makes that reuse decision collective specifically because the local-cache version permits a rank-divergent register sequence that hangs.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖 **Comprehensive RL Parity feature checklist** (vetted for duplicates/gaps).

# RL Framework Parity Wish List

A framework-neutral checklist of everything an RL framework would need to reach parity with
(and extend) the RL stack the OpenThoughts/Marin team currently relies on. Built from a
grepped, evidence-based inventory of all our SkyRL configs (current + deprecated), Leonardo
grid/launch scripts, the MarinSkyRL codebase, and the MoE/router-replay design corpus.

**Legend** — current state in *our present stack*:
✅ have-and-rely-on · ⚠️ partial / exercised but not hardened / experimental · ❌ want-but-missing

> This is a "what we want in an RL framework" parity list, not advocacy for any one framework.
> Items are checkboxes for tracking; the ✅/⚠️/❌ annotates where we are today.

---

## Core RL algorithms
- [ ] ✅ GRPO (group-relative advantage, std-normalization toggle)
- [ ] ✅ RLOO and **RLOO-N** (leave-one-out baseline that excludes masked samples; min-group-size + zero-variance-group filtering) — our production default
- [ ] ✅ REINFORCE++ and GAE (with a critic/value head)
- [ ] ✅ Pluggable advantage-estimator + policy-loss **registries** (register custom variants without forking)
- [ ] ✅ PPO clip (`regular`) and asymmetric clip (low/high ε) with **dual-clip** (OpenHands-style, high≈0.28)
- [ ] ✅ **GSPO** (group sequence policy optimization, sequence-mean reduction)
- [ ] ⚠️ SAPO / CISPO / clip-cov / kl-cov policy losses (implemented; not yet exercised by us)
- [ ] ✅ `no_op` advantage + importance-sampling loss path (for distillation objectives)
- [ ] ❌ Critic-based PPO actually run at scale (we are value-free; GAE/critic exists but unused)

## Model architectures
### Dense
- [ ] ✅ Dense transformer RL (Qwen3-8B / 32B, Qwen2.5, Qwen3-1.7B) on FSDP2
- [ ] ✅ FSDP2 training backend (sharding, reshard-after-forward, CPU/param offload)
- [ ] ⚠️ DeepSpeed backend (implemented; not our production path)
- [ ] ⚠️ Megatron 5D-parallel backend (TP/PP/CP/EP/ETP) — implemented upstream, **never launched by us** (one untested design-artifact config)
- [ ] ✅ YaRN / rope-scaling for long context (131k); FP8 weights/sync
- [ ] ⚠️ LoRA RL (config surface present, unused)

### MoE — the big gap to harden
- [ ] ⚠️ MoE RL training at all (Mixtral-8x7B, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, GLM-4.6 teacher) — exercised, not hardened
- [ ] ⚠️ **Expert Parallelism (EP)** on a non-Megatron (FSDP2/DTensor) mesh — ported (Stages 4–7), torch-backend all-to-all validated, 80B capstone step reached
- [ ] ⚠️ **Grouped-GEMM** expert compute (vs eager per-expert Python loop)
- [ ] ❌ **DeepEP** fused dispatch/combine at scale (NVSHMEM; aarch64/cu13 wheel an open risk — torch-EP is the fallback floor)
- [ ] ⚠️ **Qwen3-Next hybrid arch** (GatedDeltaNet linear-attention + 512-expert top-10 + shared expert) end-to-end RL — capstone training step done, multi-step stability still being hardened
- [ ] ⚠️ Qwen3-MoE / standard-attention MoE families
- [ ] ❌ MoE on the Megatron path for our hybrid arch (AutoBridge support for GatedDeltaNet is an open unknown)
- [ ] ❌ MoE aux/load-balancing loss in the RL loss (deliberately *not* wired — reward grads should flow to high-reward experts; flag for future optional router-bias update)

### Router replay (R3) — a desired MoE-correctness feature
- [ ] ⚠️ **Rollout Routing Replay (R3, arXiv 2510.11370)**: replay the rollout's per-token expert selection in the training forward (force top-k; keep gating gradients from live logits) so π_old == π_train for the MoE
- [ ] ⚠️ routed_experts **capture rail**: inference engine emits `[gen_len, num_layers, top_k]` over the OpenAI `/v1` API → rollout harness `extra` → trainer batch, token-aligned through sample packing + hybrid (non-uniform MoE-layer) layouts
- [ ] ⚠️ Replay correctness under sample packing and under EP all-to-all permute (per-token index alignment)
- [ ] ⚠️ Gradient-checkpointing × router-replay recompute-safety
- [ ] ❌ R3 as a first-class, framework-native feature (today it's a port/patch everywhere — not in megatron.core)

## Sync / async training
- [ ] ✅ Synchronous colocated training (policy+gen on shared GPUs)
- [ ] ✅ **Fully-async** disaggregated generation/training pipeline with bounded staleness (`max_staleness_steps`)
- [ ] ✅ Tunable generation-worker pool sized to engine fleet (oversubscription without trainer starvation)
- [ ] ✅ **Off-policy correction — TIS** (Truncated Importance Sampling, ratio cap) for stale/divergent rollouts
- [ ] ✅ Weight-transfer/sync modes: NCCL broadcast, CUDA-IPC (threshold-batched), FP8 fused-weight sync into the engine
- [ ] ⚠️ **StaleClip** staleness-aware regularizer (LR damping on stale + reward-concentrated batches) — exercised in ablations
- [ ] ❌ Adaptive/automatic staleness↔throughput controller (today it's hand-tuned per cluster)

## Inference / generation
- [ ] ✅ vLLM backend, colocated **and** disaggregated; engines launched locally; HTTP `/v1` endpoint for external harnesses
- [ ] ⚠️ SGLang backend (implemented; unused by us)
- [ ] ✅ Inference sharding: TP, PP, EP, DP per engine; N independent engines
- [ ] ✅ vLLM **`mp` executor backend** (non-Ray) — required where Ray Compiled-DAG deadlocks (hybrid-arch routed_experts capture)
- [ ] ✅ Engine efficiency knobs: prefix caching, chunked prefill, cudagraph vs enforce-eager, gpu-memory-utilization, max_num_seqs / max_num_batched_tokens, kv-cache dtype, quantization (AWQ/marlin), custom chat templates
- [ ] ✅ **routed_experts emission over `/v1`** (our `mlfoundations/vllm` fork + HTTP serialization patch) for R3 capture
- [ ] ✅ Per-token rollout logprob capture from the engine (required for TIS)
- [ ] ✅ Interleaved-thinking chat template that preserves `<think>` blocks across turns
- [ ] ✅ Sampling control: temp/top_p/top_k/min_p/repetition_penalty, separate eval sampling, DAPO overlong filtering, zero-reward-on-non-stop

## Efficiency / scaling
- [ ] ✅ Sequence packing + micro-batching (separate forward/train micro sizes)
- [ ] ✅ Gradient checkpointing (reentrant + non-reentrant) and activation/CPU/param offload (e.g. GH200 coherent LPDDR)
- [ ] ✅ FSDP `reshard_after_forward` toggle; `fsdp_size` control
- [ ] ✅ CUDA graphs / `torch.compile` / prefix cache as tunable throughput axes
- [ ] ✅ Multinode topology: SLURM + Ray-on-container bring-up; explicit policy/ref/engine node placement
- [ ] ✅ Deterministic GPU placement to avoid policy/engine collision OOM on full clusters (strict-spread PG, per-GPU bundles, CVD masking)
- [ ] ✅ Grid-sweepable efficiency axes (tp, n_samples, train/micro batch, colocate on/off, reshard, gmu, cudagraph, engine count)
- [ ] ❌ Auto memory-profiled microbatch/recompute selection (today hand-sized per model+cluster)

## Agentic support

spillover_issues.title: Automate and test new-user onboarding

spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
🤖 ## Summary

Onboarding new users onto Iris is currently ad-hoc and high-friction, which is a drag on community engagement. This is a feature request for two complementary capabilities:

1. **More tiers of access on the Iris infra** — in particular a **sandboxed / limited-privilege user tier with lower scheduling priority**, so new or less-trusted community members can be granted constrained access without risk to production runs or the shared pools.
2. **A self-onboarding process for new users** — a form-driven flow where a prospective user signs any required releases/agreements and the necessary tracking info is captured automatically, so onboarding stops being a manual one-off.

The overall goal: make new-user onboarding into Iris **less ad-hoc and lower-friction**, to support broader community engagement while keeping the cluster safe.

## 1. Tiered access (sandboxed, limited-privilege, lower-priority)

Today access is effectively all-or-nothing. A constrained tier would let us say "yes" to community users quickly. Desired properties:

- **Lower scheduling priority** — sandboxed-tier jobs yield to production/interactive work (preempted first, scheduled last), so onboarding a new user can't starve real runs.
- **Limited privileges / resource caps** — per-user or per-tier quotas (max concurrent jobs, max TPU slice size/type, max wall-clock), and restricted access to sensitive buckets/secrets/clusters.
- **Isolation** — sandboxed users can't see or affect other users' jobs/data; ideally a constrained namespace.
- Tiers should be easy for an admin to assign/upgrade (e.g. promote a sandboxed user to standard once vetted).

(Implementation is up to the Iris owners — priority classes / scale-group limits / per-user quotas already exist in spirit; this asks for a first-class "sandboxed community" tier built on them.)

## 2. Self-onboarding flow

Replace the manual back-and-forth with a form a prospective user fills out that:

- Collects the identity/affiliation info the admin (Isaac) needs to **track** the user (name, affiliation, contact, intended use, sponsor/referrer).
- Has them **sign any required releases / usage agreements** as part of the flow.
- On submission, routes everything to Isaac (and/or provisions a sandboxed-tier account) so onboarding is one self-service step instead of ad-hoc DMs.

Net effect: a new community member can request access, sign what they need to sign, and land in the sandboxed tier with minimal admin toil.

## Why now
Community interest in Iris is growing; the current ad-hoc path doesn't scale and creates friction for both newcomers and admins. A constrained tier + self-onboarding form unblocks safe, low-effort community access.

---
*Filed on behalf of @benjaminfeuer. Assigning @Helw150 to triage / route to the Iris infra owners.*

With the #6095 demonstration, it seems viable to integrate Ray based tooling like deepseek/smallpond without requiring a fork. This would add a distributed analytics engine support to Marin which we're lacking today. (Apache Ballista is a similar project in this area).

It would be nice to add this as an builtin "system service" which is launched by default by Iris at boot - this would allow users to do smaller ad-hoc queries against our data, stats, or logs without starting a new job.

# Research

Scope is "wire smallpond into Marin as a default Iris system service", which depends on PR #6095 (fakeray) landing first and requires a design decision about what "system service" means here (long-lived shared executor vs. per-query actor cohort). No code exists today; this is a greenfield integration, not a fix.

Prior art / dependencies:
- [#6095](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/6095) — fakeray Ray-Core shim on Fray; smallpond end-to-end already demoed (`/rav/sp-bigjob`). Prerequisite — not yet merged, not in the uv workspace.
- [#5861](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5861) — zephyr Dataset reading SQL via DataFusion. Overlapping intent (ad-hoc SQL over data), different layer (Dataset I/O, not a cluster service).

**Relevant code**
- [`endpoints.py#L48`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/endpoints.py#L48) — `/system/...` endpoint registry, currently only `log-server`
- [`controller.py#L570-L573`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/controller.py#L570-L573) — boot-time system-endpoint registration
- [`controller.py#L476-L521`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/controller.py#L476-L521) — `_start_local_log_server` is the template for an in-process bundled system service
- [`service.py#L1656-L1700`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/service.py#L1656-L1700) — `list_endpoints` resolves `/system/*` from the in-memory map

# Proposed Approach (for human review — do not implement until decided)

Open questions to resolve before writing code:

1. **Service shape.** Smallpond is a driver-orchestrated DAG runner, not a long-running query server. Two options:
   - **(a) Persistent SQL gateway**: a `/system/analytics` endpoint that accepts SQL, runs it via smallpond on a shared (preemptible TPU host or CPU) actor pool, returns results. Needs a query frontend, result paging, concurrency/cost limits, auth.
   - **(b) Pre-warmed actor pool only**: Iris boots a small named smallpond/fakeray actor pool; users submit jobs that attach to it instead of paying cold-start. No new RPC surface — just a documented `ray.get_actor("/system/analytics-pool")` handle.

   (b) is much smaller and matches how `/system/log-server` is used (resolve → connect). (a) is what the issue text implies ("ad-hoc queries against our data, stats, or logs without starting a new job") and is closer to Ballista.

2. **What does it actually query?** Issue mentions "data, stats, or logs". Stats/logs are already in finelog/DuckDB ([`controller.py#L495`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/controller.py#L495)) — finelog's `StatsServiceImpl` is already a SQL surface over cluster stats. Smallpond's win is parquet on `gs://`. So the actual gap is "query our parquet datasets" — overlapping with #5861 (DataFusion in zephyr Dataset). We should pick one engine for cross-parquet SQL, not ship both.

3. **Default-on cost.** Booting analytics workers on every Iris cluster (including small dev/test clusters) burns quota. Default-off behind a cluster-config flag is safer; "system service" framing should not mean "always running".

4. **Boot ordering.** fakeray needs Fray actors; Fray actors need the controller scheduling loop ([`controller.py#L532`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/controller.py#L532)) and a worker pool. The controller boots before any worker. The "system service" cannot literally start in the controller process the way `log-server` does — it needs the autoscaler to bring up its workers first. This is a real lifecycle wrinkle.

Suggested minimal first step (if approved): land (b) — a config-gated `/system/analytics-pool` registered after autoscaler bootstrap, exposing a pre-warmed fakeray actor pool. Defer (a) until there is a concrete user demanding the RPC surface. Coordinate with #5861 owner on engine choice before writing either.

Blocking on: maintainer decision on (a) vs (b), engine-choice alignment with #5861, default-on policy.

spillover_issues.author: rjpower
spillover_issues.body:
We want to make it easier to write flexibly scheduled jobs to take advantage of whatever hardware resources are available. 

Iris already allows users to manually specify a set of TPUs hardware they can run on, e.g. `or(tpuv5p-8, tpuv6e-16)`, but this requires manually identifying the hardware you want to run on, and is difficult to use properly.

We want to instead introduce device-agnostic scheduling constraints for accelerator _resources_, and use those by default for job-scheduling. This should provide enough structure for users to exclude devices that are technically correct but would have deeply pessimal performance (v5e-128 vs v5p-8).

Straw-man configuration might look something like:

```python
JobConfig.with_tpu(
  hbm="128g",
  flops_per_chip="100t",
  max_chips=32,
  max_vms=4,
)
```

This provides enough information for Iris to identify an appropriate set of TPU topologies which can satisfy this job, while preventing going way off the users desired setup.

Levanter/JAX by default infer the topology so they should work today without modification, though users may want to adjust model parameters (EP/MP/FSDP) based on the physical topology. Ideally we can auto-configure reasonable values by default.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read issue and skill docs
- [x] Surveyed existing constraint/topology code
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (no overlapping PR/issue found)
- [x] Post research + proposed approach
- [ ] Await human review before implementation (scope > 100 LOC, multi-module, new API)

**Research**

Today users hard-code a `device-variant` (`TpuDevice.variant`), and Iris already supports an `IN`-style multi-variant constraint that gives the requested `or(v5p-8, v6e-16)` behavior — but only at the granularity of named slices. The topology table at [`tpu_topology.py#L27-L71`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/tpu_topology.py#L27-L71) carries `chip_count / host_count / vm_count / chips_per_vm`, with **no per-chip HBM or FLOPs**, so there is nothing for a resource-style request to match against. The validator at [`constraints.py#L718-L795`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/constraints.py#L718-L795) already enforces that all candidate variants share `vm_count` and `chips_per_vm` (the VM is indivisible), which constrains how a resource-based request can be expanded.

**Relevant code**
- [`tpu_topology.py#L17-L71`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/tpu_topology.py#L17-L71) — `TpuTopologyInfo` table; needs HBM/FLOPs fields
- [`types.py#L424-L453`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/types.py#L424-L453) — `tpu_device(variant, count)` factory; only entry point today
- [`types.py#L505-L534`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/types.py#L505-L534) — `ResourceSpec`; needs a resource-style constructor
- [`constraints.py#L354-L375`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/constraints.py#L354-L375) — `device_variant_constraint([...])` builds the `IN` constraint used as `or(...)`
- [`constraints.py#L718-L795`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/constraints.py#L718-L795) — `validate_tpu_request`; alternatives must share `vm_count` and `chips_per_vm`
- [`types.py#L697-L729`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/types.py#L697-L729) — `adjust_tpu_replicas`; auto-fans replicas by `vm_count`

**Proposed approach**

Resource-style scheduling is a thin shim over the existing variant-IN mechanism. Three changes, in order:

1. **Extend the topology table.** Add `hbm_bytes_per_chip: int` and `flops_per_chip: float` (bf16 peak) to `TpuTopologyInfo`. Source values from the public docs links already cited above each family. Keep them on the variant rows so the topology table stays the single source of truth.

2. **Add a `TpuRequest` dataclass.** Per AGENTS guidance against `default_*` wrappers and boolean dispatch, model this as a real dataclass:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class TpuRequest:
    min_hbm_per_chip: int    # bytes; parse "128g" at construction
    min_flops_per_chip: float
    max_chips: int
    max_vms: int | None = None
    families: tuple[str, ...] = ()   # optional allowlist: ("v5p", "v6e")

    def candidate_variants(self) -> list[str]: ...
```

`candidate_variants()` filters `TPU_TOPOLOGIES` by the four constraints, then groups by `(vm_count, chips_per_vm)` and returns the largest group whose chip count is <= `max_chips`. Grouping is required because `validate_tpu_request` rejects mixed VM shapes.

3. **Wire it into job submission.** Add `ResourceSpec.with_tpu(request: TpuRequest)` (or `JobConfig.with_tpu(...)` per the straw-man) that:
   - picks a primary variant (smallest in the candidate set) for `TpuDevice.variant` so `chips_per_vm` is populated for `adjust_tpu_replicas`,
   - sets `device.tpu.count = chips_per_vm`,
   - emits a `device_variant_constraint(candidates)` attached to `IrisClient.submit_job(..., constraints=...)`.

No controller-side changes are required: the scheduler already matches `device-variant IN [...]`, and `validate_tpu_request` already rejects bad expansions.

**Open design questions before I implement**

1. **FLOPs units / dtype.** Pick one canonical metric (bf16 peak, dense, per chip). Tentative values: v4 ~275 TF, v5e ~197 TF, v5p ~459 TF, v6e ~918 TF. Per-chip + `max_chips` is simpler than aggregate `min_total_flops` — agree?
2. **API surface.** `ResourceSpec.with_tpu(TpuRequest(...))` (composable, dataclass-first) vs `JobConfig.with_tpu(hbm=..., flops_per_chip=..., max_chips=..., max_vms=...)` (matches the straw-man, more discoverable). Lean dataclass; want the straw-man kwargs form as a thin wrapper?
3. **Auto-topology hints to Levanter.** Issue says "ideally auto-configure EP/MP/FSDP". That is a Levanter-side mesh inference concern; suggest deferring out of this PR — Iris just narrows the candidate set, Levanter infers mesh at runtime.
4. **Default when no constraints are given.** Should an unannotated training job get a model-aware default (`min_hbm_per_chip >= params * dtype / dp`)? Probably out of scope until we have a model-aware helper.

Estimated size: ~150 LOC across `tpu_topology.py`, `types.py`, plus tests in `lib/iris/tests/`. Will open a PR once #1 and #2 are decided.

## Description

Follow-up from #5815. The BF16 B200 baseline/profile goal is complete, but the fair-fit d5120/L8 result shows Grug still trails the Megatron TE + flash + native DeepEP profile after the attention-specific work landed.

Relevant #5815 numbers:

| run | profile-window tok/s | post-profile tok/s |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Grug d5120/L8, `ragged_all_to_all` | 14,068.57 | 14,230.55 |
| Grug d5120/L8, ring/all-gather comparator | 24,007.82 | 24,350.55 |
| Megatron d5120/L8, TE + flash + native DeepEP | 86,197.25 | 91,574.88 |

The ring/all-gather comparator is about 1.71x faster than `ragged_all_to_all`, so `ragged_all_to_all` is a real bottleneck. It is not the whole gap: the best Grug comparator remains about 3.76x below the Megatron post-profile throughput.

## Scope

B200 BF16, d5120/L8, EP=8, batch=8, seq_len=4096. This issue should focus on Grug MoE transport/combine and the whole-step effects of the transport choice. Attention-only work is tracked separately in #6039 and was integrated through #6059/#6069.

- Identify the Grug MoE transport/combine wall-time contribution for the d5120/L8 B200 profile cell.
- Compare `ragged_all_to_all`, ring/all-gather, and any candidate DeepEP-equivalent or fused transport path on the same shape.
- Land only the smallest scoped implementation or harness change needed to make the candidate path reproducible.
- Post before/after post-profile tok/s and profile-window tok/s with artifact links.
- State the remaining gap to the Megatron d5120/L8 profile after the transport change.

- Parent baseline/profile closeout: #5815
- Existing dispatch/combine issue: #5609
- Existing local GMM/MLP epic: #5328

# Research

Three Grug EP backends already live in [`lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe), selected via `implementation=` in [`grug_moe.py#L208-L215`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/grug_moe.py#L208-L215). Per #5815, `ragged_all_to_all` lands at 14.2k tok/s on d5120/L8 B200, `ring` at 24.4k tok/s, vs Megatron TE+DeepEP at 91.6k tok/s. The DeepEP backend exists in Grug ([`ep_deepep.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_deepep.py)) and has SM100/B200 build paths wired in [`availability.py#L35`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/kernels/deepep/availability.py#L35) and [`#L213`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/kernels/deepep/availability.py#L213) but **does not appear in the #5815 results table** — the gap to Megatron may largely be that the Grug DeepEP path has not been measured/optimized for d5120/L8 yet.

**Relevant code**
- [`grug_moe.py#L199-L243`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/grug_moe.py#L199-L243) — EP backend dispatch (ring/raa/deepep) under shard_map
- [`ep_ragged_all_to_all.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ragged_all_to_all.py) — current default; two `jax.lax.ragged_all_to_all` per layer + repermute
- [`ep_deepep.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_deepep.py) — DeepEP intranode dispatch/combine; calls `deepep_dispatch_intranode` / `deepep_combine_intranode`
- [`ep_ring.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring.py) — all-gather + psum-scatter; the 1.71x faster comparator
- [`_moe/common.py#L31`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/common.py#L31) — `_EP_MOE_IMPLEMENTATIONS = (\"ring\", \"ragged_all_to_all\", \"deepep\")`

# Proposed Approach

Why this is not a self-contained fix: closing the gap requires (a) running the existing Grug `deepep` backend on B200 at d5120/L8/EP=8 with the validated DeepEP commit `7febc6e25`, (b) producing JAX/Perfetto profiles, (c) likely 1–N rounds of kernel/layout work on whichever path wins. None of (a)/(b)/(c) is reachable from CI; the issue's Definition of Done is built around B200 throughput numbers.

Suggested ordering for whoever picks this up (in priority order, smallest scope first):

1. **Measure first, code second.** Run the existing `implementation=\"deepep\"` Grug path on the same d5120/L8 cell pinned in #5815 with `DEEPEP_CUDA_ARCH=sm_100` and `DEEPEP_SRC_ROOT` at the validated commit. If it materially closes the gap, the only remaining work may be wiring it as the default for B200 + a runbook entry; that is a true small PR. The fair-fit table in #5815 not listing the `deepep` Grug cell is the central missing data point.

2. **If `deepep` underperforms vs Megatron's native DeepEP, profile to attribute the gap** between three buckets: (i) FFI launch / Python-side packing in `_pack_deepep_local_assignments` ([`ep_deepep.py#L43-L77`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_deepep.py#L43-L77)) — note this uses `top_k(assignments)` + `take`, which is exactly the scatter/gather pattern flagged in #5609; (ii) intranode CUDA kernel time; (iii) the `segment_sum` collapse in `_collapse_deepep_local_assignments`. The packing/collapse layer is the most likely Grug-side hot path and is a JAX-only fix (no CUDA).

3. **Whole-step effects of transport choice.** The issue explicitly asks for whole-step, not just transport, deltas. The `ring` backend keeps tokens replicated globally and uses `psum_scatter` ([`ep_ring.py#L109-L113`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring.py#L109-L113)), trading memory for kernel simplicity — at d5120/L8/EP=8 this works because tokens-per-shard fits, but it will not scale to larger EP. Land the per-transport measurement table before optimizing further so the choice is grounded.

4. **Harness change (smallest landable piece).** A reproducible harness that runs the three backends back-to-back on the d5120/L8 shape and writes the throughput table + Perfetto artifacts. This is the one piece that could land independently as a small PR; it would unblock everyone else and matches the \"smallest scoped implementation or harness change\" wording in the DoD. Likely lives next to existing Grug profile scripts (none found in `experiments/`; check internal scripts).

I have not opened a PR. The actionable next step needs a human with B200 access to either run the `deepep` Grug measurement or to scope the harness PR — I can author the harness PR if pointed at the existing profile-driver entry point used for the #5815 runs.

🤖 Tracking issue filed per dlwh's review comment on #4637 (`lib/levanter/src/levanter/adaptor/lora.py`).

## Problem

LoRA currently excludes `lm_head` by default — `LoraConfig.exclude_modules` defaults to `["lm_head"]`. Every model's `get_lm_head()` accesses `self.lm_head.weight` directly, which breaks when `lm_head` is a `LoraLinear` (it has no `.weight`; the base weight lives at `.wrapped.weight`). `resize_vocab()` makes the same `.weight` assumption.

## Proposed fix

Update `get_lm_head()` in all model classes (`llama`, `qwen`, `gemma`, `mixtral`, `olmo`, `olmo3`, `apertus`, `mistral`) to handle `LoraLinear`, e.g.:

```python
if isinstance(self.lm_head, LoraLinear):
    return self.lm_head.wrapped.weight
```

and fix the same `.weight` assumption in `resize_vocab()`. Then `lm_head` can be dropped from the default `exclude_modules`, enabling LoRA on `lm_head` (which some research suggests is beneficial — Thinking Machines 2025, "apply LoRA to all weight matrices").

## Acceptance

- `get_lm_head()` and `resize_vocab()` handle `LoraLinear` across all listed model classes.
- A model loraized with `lm_head` included passes forward / merge / HF export.
- `lm_head` removed from the default `exclude_modules` (or documented why it must stay).

## References

- #4637 review comment (dlwh) on `lib/levanter/src/levanter/adaptor/lora.py`.
- The `TODO(IMPORTANT)` next to `exclude_modules` in that file.

spillover_issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This epic tracks the attempt to make Grug's local MoE expert MLP path fast by adapting SonicMoE ideas into a JAX-callable Marin backend. The investigation narrowed from broad Sonic/QuACK custom-call options to the local grouped `w13` / activation / grouped `w2` path and gather/combine behavior on GH200/H200-class GPUs. By mid-May 2026, plain JAX/Pallas paths had shown useful forward performance but not enough backward/remat improvement; the production-facing direction then narrowed to PR #5718's `implementation="sonic"` backend, which keeps existing JAX `ragged_dot` grouped GEMMs and ports Sonic's token gather/combine kernel through `jax-triton` with a custom VJP. The remaining work is to validate that backend in realistic GPU training shapes and keep the more fragile CuTe/QuACK ragged-TMA experiments as research notes, not default production dependencies.

### Helpful links
- Latest production-path update: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5328#issuecomment-4484868494
- PR #5718 scope update: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5328#issuecomment-4484780037
- jax-triton train-step comparison: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5328#issuecomment-4449166706
- CuTe/QuACK ragged-TMA reproducer result: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5328#issuecomment-4453791007
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Goal

Produce and land a local MoE kernel backend for GH200/H200-class NVIDIA GPUs that materially improves Grug's local expert MLP path on the authoritative GPU benchmark cells, with a clear interface boundary against the transport layer.

Success target for this research thread: find a JAX-callable path, or a custom-call path usable from JAX, that gets within roughly 10-20% of Sonic/QuACK on the local MoE block.

## Scope

In scope:
- local grouped `w13` / activation / grouped `w2` path
- local gather-and-sum / combine behavior
- activation-memory-efficient local backward bookkeeping where it matters
- Pallas, Mosaic GPU, custom-call, or direct Sonic/QuACK wrapper routes that can be called from JAX
- comparisons against `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/grug_moe.py`

Out of scope:
- DeepEP-equivalent dispatch/return transport
- ring vs `ragged_all_to_all` transport design
- broad PyTorch interop layers unrelated to a measured local-kernel win
- router/top-k redesign unless a local kernel requires a narrowly scoped metadata change

## Current Baseline

Primary GH200 shape: `tokens=8192`, `hidden=2048`, `intermediate=3072`, `experts=8`, `topk=2`, BF16.

| Measure | Real Sonic/QuACK | Best JAX/Grug path so far | Gap |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| forward | `1.260ms` | `1.285ms` | `+2.0%` |
| `fwd_bwd` | `3.428ms` | `4.035ms` | `+17.7%` |
| `fwd2_bwd` proxy | `4.428ms` | `5.640ms` | `+27.4%` |
| `remat_bwd` / checkpoint | `4.798ms` | `5.844ms` with `prevent_cse=True` | `+21.8%` |

Interpretation:
- Use `fwd_bwd` for ordinary no-remat training comparisons.
- Use `remat_bwd` with `prevent_cse=True` for honest forced-recompute comparisons.
- Do not use the older JAX `remat_bwd=4.056ms` number for parity claims; that used `prevent_cse=False` and appears to have benefited from XLA CSE/reuse across the checkpoint boundary.

## Latest Update

Latest issue comment: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5328#issuecomment-4484868494

Latest local logbook entries:
- `.agents/logbooks/sonicmoe-jax-triton-overhead.md`: raw Sonic jax-triton gather/combine train-step probes
- `.agents/logbooks/sonicmoe-pallas-grug.md`, `SONIC-PALLAS-044`: CuTe DSL JAX integration smoke and follow-up ragged-TMA blockers

Local handoff: `/Users/dlwh/src/marin/scratch/moe-block-decomposition-handoff-20260513.md`

## Decision Log

- 2026-04-30: narrowed the broad SonicMoE scout to this local-compute epic for Grug MoE GMM/MLP.
- 2026-05-10: Pallas unpack-backward VJP produced a small real training win, about `2.8%` end-to-end on the 006a-style 1x GH200 synthetic run.
- 2026-05-11: full forward path is close enough to Sonic; the remaining question moved to full-block backward and remat behavior.
- 2026-05-12: direct Mosaic GPU vector-indexed metadata/gather path hit JAX lowering blockers; scalar Mosaic workaround lowered but did not close the Sonic gap.
- 2026-05-13: full-block comparison shows best JAX no-remat path is `+17.7%` vs Sonic, but honest remat is `+21.8%` vs Sonic.
- 2026-05-13: naive activation+W13 Pallas/Triton fusion was rejected. It avoids materializing `d_w13_out` but recomputes the SwiGLU derivative across many matmul tiles and runs at `29.361ms` vs `1.836ms` for the materialized baseline.
- 2026-05-13: pure JAX whole-local-MoE `custom_vjp` scaffold was rejected as a speed path. It is locally correct and useful as an ABI scaffold, but full-shape GH200 timing was `12.804ms fwd_bwd` and `14.430ms remat_bwd`, far slower than `sonic_xla`.
- 2026-05-13: Sonic/QuACK down-projection backward bridge succeeded on GH200. JAX-owned tensors via zero-copy DLPack ran the down-backward bucket at `1.008ms` for the full shape, making it a credible custom-call target rather than a production bridge by itself.
- 2026-05-13: CuTe DSL through `cutlass.jax.cutlass_call` succeeded on the GH200 worker (`max_abs=0`, `0.118ms` steady for a vector-add smoke), so the source-level CuTe/JAX port path is available.
- 2026-05-14: raw Sonic jax-triton gather/combine with a custom VJP beat the XLA combine proxy in a train-step-shaped GH200 harness, but the QuACK/CuTe down-backward path hit `Unexpected index` lowering failures.
- 2026-05-19: PR #5718 was narrowed to production-visible `implementation="sonic"`: existing concat W13 layout and JAX `ragged_dot` grouped GEMMs, plus raw Sonic jax-triton gather/combine. CuTe/QuACK dependencies and pseudo-Sonic XLA/down-gather public backends were removed from that PR.

## Negative Results Index

- Full W13 custom VJP around the expert-padded path was too broad and slow; the narrower unpack-backward VJP was the useful part. See https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5328#issuecomment-4416373304 and https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5328#issuecomment-4416387690.
- Isolated gather/sum Pallas Triton variants, including faithful source ports and inline PTX arithmetic, did not match real Sonic. The remaining gap persisted even in a standalone Marin-free repro and showed worse SASS/register/control-instruction characteristics for Pallas.
- Directly launching the exact Sonic Triton cubin through JAX FFI worked functionally but carried an approximately fixed `56-60us` launch tax, erasing the Sonic advantage for the isolated gather/sum kernel.
- Mosaic GPU high-level vector indexing currently hits JAX lowering blockers for the relevant metadata/gather forms. Scalar `plgpu.load` workarounds lower but are tied-to-slower than Pallas Triton and remain slower than real Sonic.
- JAX checkpoint/remat with `prevent_cse=False` gave a misleading `4.056ms` result. With `prevent_cse=True`, the best JAX remat path is `5.844ms`.
- Naive activation+W13 fusion in Pallas/Triton is a dead end for this shape: fused `dx` and `dw` subkernels are `14-15ms` each because they recompute the activation derivative per matmul tile.
- Pure JAX whole-MoE `custom_vjp` does not improve schedule quality by itself. The corrected scaffold ran `12.804ms fwd_bwd` and `14.430ms remat_bwd`; making W2 transposes explicit was worse.
- QuACK/CuTe ragged TMA is fragile in this integration. The d-gated epilogue has a two-extra-dim encoding workaround, but the production PR removed the CuTe/QuACK dependency path rather than relying on it.

## Current Conclusion

Forward-only performance and isolated combine microbenchmarks are no longer the main decision point. The practical production path is the narrowed `implementation="sonic"` backend from PR #5718: concat W13 layout, existing JAX `ragged_dot` grouped GEMMs, and raw Sonic jax-triton gather/combine with a custom VJP. The CuTe/QuACK custom-call route remains useful research context but is too fragile for the current production PR. Next work should validate the sonic backend on real GPU training shapes and resolve any remaining robustness issues before treating it as a default MoE path.

🤖 Milestone update for the GH200 Sonic-equivalent JAX path (`SONIC-PALLAS-046`, logbook: `.agents/logbooks/sonicmoe-pallas-grug.md`).

Shape/hardware: `T=8192,H=2048,I=3072,E=8,topk=2,BF16` on `coreweave-rno2a` GH200.

Current comparison:

| Path | Forward | `fwd_bwd` | honest remat |

| Real Sonic/QuACK | `1.260ms` | `3.428ms` | `4.798ms` |
| Previous best JAX/Grug | `1.285ms` | `4.035ms` | `5.844ms` |
| JAX + CuTe QuACK down-bwd (`sonic_xla_cutlass_down`) | `~1.285ms` | `3.998ms` | `5.103ms` |

What changed:
- The source-level `cutlass.jax.cutlass_call` port of QuACK down-backward is full speed in isolation: `0.956ms` for `dgated + dw2` at the full shape.
- The first whole-MoE custom VJP attempt was a negative result: `12.599ms` `fwd_bwd`, `14.048ms` `fwd2_bwd`, and remat hit `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_ADDRESS`.
- The useful path is now granular: keep normal JAX/XLA dispatch, forward, and W13 backward, but wrap only `activation -> down ragged_dot -> gather_sum` in a custom VJP whose backward launches the QuACK CuTe calls.
- After setting `allow_cuda_graph=False` on the custom calls, `remat_bwd` succeeds at `5.103ms`. `fwd_bwd` remeasured at `3.998ms`, about `16.6%` behind real Sonic and inside the target band.

Open blocker:
- `fwd2_bwd` still fails with `Failed to set CUDA graph kernel node params: CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_ADDRESS` when the extra forward and custom-call backward coexist in one compiled graph. Disabling CUDA graph capture fixed remat but not fwd2, so this looks like a layout/alias/custom-call contract problem rather than ordinary dispatch overhead.

Interpretation:
- This is the first JAX-in-XLA path that reaches the desired speed band for backward/remat, but I would not call it production-ready until `fwd2_bwd` is stable.
- The remaining gap is probably not just JAX dispatch overhead. The isolated QuACK bucket is fast, but integrated savings are partly eaten by GLU interleave/deinterleave packing and residual XLA W13/backward scheduling.

Next steps:
- Inspect `cutlass.jax` `input_spec`/`output_spec`/layout controls and force the custom-call operands/results to match the CuTe views.
- Quantify full-shape GLU packing overhead directly.
- If layout fixes stabilize fwd2, keep this as the short-term JAX path; otherwise port the Sonic/QuACK W13 side or change the JAX W13 layout so the down-backward call consumes interleaved GLU activations directly.

spillover_issues.title: Epic: make local Grug MoE GMM/MLP fast via SonicMoE-style kernels

spillover_issues.author: mcwitt
spillover_issues.body:
The ragged all-to-all EP backend hangs at the d6144 hero scale (11 racks, 704 GPUs) within the first hundred steps, on both attempts of the 2026-09-02 deployment. The train step never completes on one rack, the other ten spin in the next AllReduce, and levanter's progress watchdog kills the gang 15 minutes later (`No progress after train_step_started for 909.8 seconds (timeout 900.0); terminating with exit code 124`). No rank logs an error: nothing from NCCL, XLA, CUDA (no Xid), the allocator, or Kubernetes. The hero was rolled back to `04751985c7` (pooled-wave backend), which resumed cleanly from the same checkpoint.

Deployment: main `8e48cdb3ca`, run `hero-ragged_a2a-ep-step54k` resuming `hero-12d8b6f0-dee637` from its `step-54000` permanent checkpoint (#8868), `HERO_WATCH_INTERVAL = 10`, `--xla_gpu_experimental_ragged_all_to_all_use_device_kernel=true --xla_enable_nccl_symmetric_buffers_for_collectives=raggedalltoall`, jax 0.11.1, NCCL 2.30.7. Coordinator `/marin/hero-ragged_a2a-ep-step54k-coord-aade2815`; both attempts ran on the same 176 nodes.

- Attempt 0: steps 54001–54070 completed normally (loss tracks the pooled-wave run step for step at −0.006 nats, drops 3.4e-2 → <1e-4, MFU 20.5 → 23.4%, peak HBM 103.6 GiB). Step 54071 started at 00:23:30Z and never finished; killed 00:38:46Z.
- Attempt 1: restored the same checkpoint, completed step 54000 at 00:45:38Z (loss 1.2364, identical to attempt 0), then hung on step 54001; killed ~01:01Z.

Both hangs are on the first plain train step after a `diagnostic_watch_step` step (54070 → 54071 after seven clean alternations; 54000 → 54001 on the first). The plain and watch steps are two XLA executables that share the NCCL symmetric-memory arena for the ragged all-to-all: each registers its own window at the arena base (`AcquireSymmetricMemory`, `CollectiveMemoryCache`), and equal footprints coexist. #8861 is the same design failing the other way: an executable with a *different* footprint (the capacity-limited eval) makes the next train step fail with `ncclGroupEnd() failed: invalid argument`. Here the footprints are equal and the failure is a silent hang instead of an error, so #8859 (dropless eval only) removes the crash but not this.

Evidence that the hang sits on one rack's EP domain rather than a node fault:

- NCCL RAS (periodic `STATUS` from process 0, `telemetry_v1.levanter`): six minutes into each hang, 64 cross-rack communicators show an AllReduce operation-count skew of exactly 3 (attempt 0: min 10509 / max 10512 at 00:29:43Z; attempt 1: 190 / 193 at 00:52:30Z) and the 704-rank communicator a skew of 2. Before the hangs every communicator was in sync. One member per cross-rack communicator behind by the same count is one whole rack that never entered the step's trailing AllReduces.
- Iris per-task CPU (`iris.task`): exactly 16 of 176 tasks ran at ~4.0 cores while the other 160 ran at ~8.0 during each hang, i.e. one rack in a different wait state from the ranks busy-polling in AllReduce. Attempt 0: tasks 128–143 (zone 129, nodes `s38vxs64 s45sxs64 s51vxs64 s5xvxs64 s69vxs64 s7htxs64 s7qvxs64 s8ktxs64 s8mtxs64 s8yvxs64 s9jvxs64 s9lrxs64 scspxs64 scssxs64 sd8sxs64 shmsxs64`). Attempt 1: tasks 64–79, a different rack on the same node set.
- py-spy thread dumps (`iris process profile threads`) of tasks 0, 83, and 140 during attempt 0: every rank's main thread inside `train_step` (`train.py:1176`), no Python-side wait; the hang is below XLA's dispatch.
- No node conditions or events on either rack; the cluster's six `HPCVerification=Fail` nodes are elsewhere.

The stall-triggered verbose RAS capture (`trigger = stall`) published nothing in either attempt, so the rank-level view that would name the stuck ranks and the pending collective is missing; the periodic sample is all we have. Neither a 200-step 1-rack smoke restoring the same checkpoint (20 watch/plain alternations) nor the 11,420-step d768 rung reproduced it, so the failure needs more than one rack, i.e. more than one EP domain sharing the job.

Side observations from the same deployment: a cold compile at this shape took 22.9 min for the watch executable plus 6.6 min for the plain one; the data loader's second 64-item prefetch took 920 s (overlapped by compile) where the pooled-wave hero's restarts took under 100 s.

Done when: the ragged backend runs at 11 racks through at least several hundred steps with watch steps enabled without a hang, or the hang is reproduced at smaller multi-rack scale with a GPU-side stack (CUDA core dump / `cuda-gdb` on a stuck rank) that names the kernel or collective.

Related: #8861 (symmetric-window overlap between executables), #8859, #8868, #8506 (hero status log). Side-by-side trial report: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/ep_change:-hero-ragged-a2a-swap,-200-step-trial--VmlldzoxNzg1ODIzMA==

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 The mechanism this issue describes is not what the hung run did, and the root cause is still open. Recording what has been ruled out so the next attempt does not repeat it.

The hero had one train executable, not two alternating ones. `launch_scaling_ladder.py:216` sets `WatchMode.INLINE` at the deployed commit `8e48cdb3ca`, so `_make_diagnostic_watch_step` is never built (`train.py:906`), `jit_train_step` computes watch stats on every step, and `step % 10 == 0` only decides whether the host logs them. Step 54071 was byte-identical to 54070 at the XLA and NCCL level. The working pooled-wave hero carries the identical watch config and does not hang.

The capacity-limited evaluator was already disabled. `c3f51e5250` (#8859) is an ancestor of `8e48cdb3ca`, and the dropless evaluator uses `sonic_cute`, which has no all-to-all and registers no symmetric window.

Window aliasing is present but was not the trigger. Two `jit_train_step` executables per rank each register a window at `0xbf80000000`; the cause is now known and is a step-counter sharding mismatch (details in #8861). What turns that aliasing into the `ncclGroupEnd` error is a third executable with a smaller footprint, and no such executable was running here.

Ruled out with evidence, all on one rack at the hero's shape, data and checkpoint unless noted. GIN: the device kernel logs `lsa_size=64 num_ranks=64 gin=false cta_count=152 num_updates_per_replica=6`, and forcing `lsa_size < num_ranks` produces `Device kernel skipped: lsa_size=32 num_ranks=64 requires GIN` followed by a hard `RaggedAllToAll fallback to NCCL is not allowed`, so `SupportsGin()` is false in this configuration. That also proves every hero EP domain was a single NVLink domain, since a domain spanning two would have failed loudly rather than stalled. CTA co-residency: the LSA barrier is per-slot, not grid-cooperative — `blockIdx.x` selects a barrier slot and CTA k rendezvouses only with CTA k on its peers — and at `__launch_bounds__(128, 8)` the 152-CTA grid uses a fraction of the device, so `0de14631ea` did not regress residency and the comment in that patch claiming the whole grid must be resident is wrong. `core_count` divergence: every rank reports `cta_count=152`. Hardware: the task-index-to-node map is identical across both attempts and the two stuck 16-task slices share no node. Allocator address churn: `Buffer allocations changed address between module jit_train_step executions` fires only for `parameter` and `live-out` entries, never `temp`, so the arena backing the window is stable. Ragged metadata: `CheckRaggedAllToAllBounds` passed 160 of 160 checks on the same HLO operands the device kernel consumes. NCCL 2.31.2: tested, identical failure (see #8861).

One rack does not reproduce it. Attempts covered two 32-GPU EP domains in one rack (161 steps, clean), raised collective overlap (dies of NaN at step 2, which is #8317's corruption and a different regime), NCCL channel contention, forcing the GIN branch, and a full-fidelity control at 48 layers with mixture data restored from the same `step-54000` checkpoint. The remaining differences at eleven racks — cross-rack collectives sharing the GPUs, and a 704-rank communicator — cannot be built inside one NVLink domain.

What survives is a stall in the LSA barrier that cannot report itself. XLA calls `ncclLsaBarrierSession::sync` in the no-timeout form, and NCCL sets `abortFlag` only `if (isInternal)` (`src/dev_runtime.cc:1175`), so a user-created devComm has none and no watchdog, abort or CUDA error can fire. The barrier epoch is an absolute counter that persists across launches and is zeroed once at `ncclDevCommCreate`, so any divergence is permanent.

Three instrumentation gaps made both attempts undiagnosable, and should be fixed before the next one. The stall diagnostic is never wired: `train.py:968` calls `progress_watchdog.create(process_index=...)` with no `diagnostic=`, so `diagnostic_timeout` stays unset and the stall capture publishes nothing. If it were wired it would run on the wrong process, because `ProgressWatchdogConfig.create` returns `None` for the entire watchdog when `diagnostic_timeout` is set and `process_index != 0`. And the watchdog's `startup_grace_period` defaulted to one hour, which covered attempt 1's entire hang — that run was killed by hand, not by the watchdog.

For the next eleven-rack attempt: set `TF_CPP_MIN_LOG_LEVEL=0` alongside `TF_CPP_VMODULE=ragged_all_to_all_thunk=3,nccl_symmetric_memory=3,gpu_executable=5`, and `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO` with `NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=REG,INIT,COLL`. `TF_CPP_VMODULE` alone emits nothing, and `NCCL_DEBUG=WARN` emits nothing for this failure class. A diagnostic PJRT build on `marin-community/xla` branch `mcwitt/8870-barrier-timeout` bounds both LSA barrier waits with NCCL's timeout overloads and records the stalled rank, barrier slot and phase, so the next occurrence names itself instead of producing fifteen minutes of silence. It also builds the device kernels against the NCCL the runtime loads: `tensorflow.bazelrc` pins `HERMETIC_NCCL_VERSION=2.29.7` while the runtime installs 2.30.7, and the timeout API exists only in the newer headers.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Follow-up on one hypothesis worth keeping open: that this is the same class of bug as #8861, namely a sharding JAX infers rather than one the code specifies, going wrong only once `replica_dcn` is a real axis.

Partial test on one rack. A single rack can make that axis non-degenerate by splitting into several expert domains, so: `--expert-axis-size 32` (giving `replica_dcn=2`) with `--num-experts 192` to keep six local experts per GPU and the hero's memory profile, 48 layers, inline watch, with the #8861 step-counter fix applied. Result was 64 arena windows, 64 `jit(train_step)` compilations across 64 ranks, and a per-leaf `Format` diff reporting `identical across the step`. No second state-sharding mismatch appears when the replica axis becomes real, and the #8861 fix holds there.

That does not close the hypothesis. It covers the train state only, at replica width 2, inside one NVLink domain and one process group. It does not cover batch sharding over `_BATCH_AXES = ("replica_dcn", "data", "expert")`, intermediates inside the step, or device ordering across 704 devices in 176 processes. Ordering is the part that matters here: `compact_grug_mesh` builds the mesh by reshaping `jax.devices()` in process order, while a `GSPMDSharding` carries the client's default device order, and the two coincide trivially when `replica_dcn=1`. A disagreement that resolves differently on different racks is the only proposed source of rank-dependent behaviour that survives, which is what a failure hitting one rack of eleven — a different one on each attempt — requires.

The direct test is a dump comparison, and it was not possible before now. `hero_grug_trainer_config` left `sharding_dump_path=None`, so `dump_grug_state_sharding_run_artifact` wrote to the pod-local `logs/` directory and the hung run's dump died with its pod. The ladder now writes it under the run's output path, so the next multi-rack run leaves a dump that can be diffed against a one-rack dump directly. That needs no special build and costs nothing.

Also worth recording for anyone reproducing this: `--expert-axis-size 32` at the hero's 384 experts puts twelve local experts on each GPU instead of six and OOMs at 158 GiB. Halve the expert count to hold the per-GPU profile fixed.

comments.body:
🤖 An eleven-rack reproduction attempt on 2026-09-03 did not reproduce the hang, but it eliminated data- and state-dependence by direct measurement and turned up a version skew that reframes the failure. Root cause is still open.

**The reproduction was faithful, and it did not hang.** Two jobs at 11 racks, 235 steps in total (164 then 71), restored from the same `step-54000` both failed attempts used, at the hero's exact shape. It matched attempt 0's loss to ±0.00007 nats over the whole overlapping range and sat -0.0058 nats against the pooled-wave control, reproducing the -0.006 offset reported above; MFU 22-23% against attempt 0's 23.4%. It carried the same transport (`lsa_size=64 num_ranks=64 gin=false cta_count=152`) and the same symmetric-window aliasing this issue describes: 1408 arena-window registrations across 704 ranks, exactly two per rank, alongside 1408 `jit_train_step` compilations.

**The hang is not a function of the data or the model state.** Attempt 0 completed step 54071 (`train_loss` 1.23687 at 00:23:35.14Z) and hung on the next one. The replay ran through that step and kept going. Since the loss agrees to seven significant figures, the batch, the routing, the optimizer state and the arithmetic there are identical to the run that died. Combined with attempt 1 hanging at 54001 from the same restored state, the trigger is timing, not state, and the failure cannot be forced by choosing a checkpoint or a step.

**On the statistics, stated carefully.** Hero exposure was 75 step-attempts with two hangs; the reproduction ran 235 clean. A one-sided test gives p ≈ 0.06 — suggestive that something differs between the two setups, but not significant. Job-steps are the right unit here, not rack-steps: the hang is a job-level event, so counting all 11 racks as independent trials overstates the evidence.

**Candidates eliminated since the last update.** Concurrent checkpoint I/O: `grep "Saving checkpoint"` across every task log in both attempts returns zero hits, so neither attempt ever wrote a checkpoint. Online W&B: per-step tracker cost was 3.73-3.84 ms at every detail step and the wandb thread was idle in `selectors.select` at the py-spy dump. The NCCL RAS probe: it ran in both attempts at a 600 s cadence taking 69-83 ms, and the 00:29:43.8Z poll *succeeded during the hang*, so process 0 and NCCL's in-process listener were responsive while the gang was wedged. A rank silently falling off the device-kernel path: `RaggedAllToAllThunk::RunCollective` returns `InvalidArgument("RaggedAllToAll fallback to NCCL is not allowed")` when `xla_gpu_allow_ragged_all_to_all_nccl_send_recv_fallback` is false, which is the deployed setting, so such a rank fails loudly rather than desynchronising quietly, and no attempt logged an error. Two ragged kernels sharing barrier slots: the hero forces `--xla_gpu_experimental_parallel_collective_overlap_limit=1`, so collectives cannot be co-resident.

**The version skew, which is a real defect on its own.** `tensorflow.bazelrc:192` pins `HERMETIC_NCCL_VERSION="2.29.7"` while the runtime resolves to 2.30.7. NCCL's `ncclDevCommCompat_v22907` shim then forces `ginType = NONE` and gates `deviceApiSupport` on `ncclTeamLsa(comm).nRanks == comm->nRanks`. That explains structurally why `SupportsGin()` is false — it was never a configuration choice — and why the device kernel only ever runs on the per-rack EP64 clique, so eleven racks are eleven independent barrier domains whose hazard adds with rack count while nothing couples them. It also means the deployed kernel is compiled without 2.30's bounded `sync(..., timeoutCycles)` overload and without its system-scope release fence in `arrive`, which is exactly why the stall cannot report itself.

**Leading remaining hypothesis.** A stray peer store from the copy loop landing inside the devComm resource window and corrupting the barrier state. Every symmetric window, including the one holding the barrier epochs, lives in the same `devr` VA reservation with a common `stride4G`, and the barrier epoch is an absolute per-slot counter that is never reset or exchanged, so any divergence is permanent: a peer that falls behind makes its partner spin on a comparison that wraps to ~2^32, with `abortFlag == nullptr` for user devComms and no timeout. One sub-case has a matching upstream fix we do not carry: NCCL `0d7243b`, "Mitigate loadConst `__ldg` regression", replaces the non-coherent `__ldg` read of `lsaFlatBase`/`stride4G` with a plain dereference, and those window pointers are rewritten at run time by `ncclDevrReplaceSegmentWindowsIfNeeded`.

**Instrumentation now exists, and did not before.** `CUDA_` was missing from the dispatcher's forwarded env prefixes, so the GPU core-dump variables could never reach a training gang; with that fixed the driver creates one dump pipe per rank. A dump must be taken with `CUDA_COREDUMP_GENERATION_FLAGS=skip_abort,skip_global_memory,skip_constbank_memory`: the default writes 62 GB and SIGABRTs the process, which killed all 64 ranks of a smoke gang and lost the dump with the pod, while the flags give 283 MB. Even so it is terminal within about two minutes (measured at 2:36 and 1:55), so it must trigger, read and upload in one round trip and go last. A dump taken mid-kernel names the resident kernel and gives a per-block state table, which matters because the LSA barrier is per-slot indexed by `blockIdx.x` and that table therefore names the diverged slots directly. NCCL RAS `VERBOSE STATUS` can also be triggered by hand during a hang, answering in ~4 ms with the per-collective min/max that showed the AllReduce skew of exactly 3. Do not attach `cuda-gdb` to a live process: an attach to PID 1 returned nothing in 150 s and took the gang down.

**Next.** A wheel built with the device kernels compiled against the run-time NCCL 2.30.7 exists as `marin-xla-pjrt-candidate-ca0716a2da95`; it removes the skew, adds bounded LSA barriers that record rank, slot and phase, extends the bounds check to the device path, and promotes the transport line to INFO. It is being validated on one rack. The one structural difference between the hero and the reproduction that survives all of the above is that the hero runs `broadcast_one_to_all` inside `checkpointer.on_step` on every step — a cross-host collective on a `(176, 4)` mesh whose rank groups exist nowhere else in the job — while the reproduction, with `save_checkpoints=False`, never creates a checkpointer at all (`train.py:1031`). A next window should restore that at zero I/O cost with `--save-checkpoints --checkpoint-minutes 600`, and a one-rack `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=INIT,REG` A/B on that flag would first confirm the communicator inventory actually differs.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 One actionable gap found while testing a prediction of the barrier-stall hypothesis, worth recording separately because it is cheap to fix and independent of everything else above.

The hypothesis predicts the stuck rack's GPUs were saturated during the hang, spinning inside a resident device kernel, as opposed to idle because the kernel never launched. That is directly checkable from `iris.task`, which carries `accelerator_util_pct` and `accelerator_mem_bytes`. During attempt 0's hang window (00:23:36-00:38:43Z) **both fields are null in all 2,636 samples**.

The query is sound: the same rows reproduce the known CPU signature exactly, with the stuck rack at 4.04 cores against 7.85 on the healthy racks, matching the 4.0-vs-8.0 split reported in this issue. So the nulls are a collection gap rather than a query error.

That gap is expensive out of proportion to its size. GPU utilisation separates "spinning in a resident kernel" from "kernel never launched" on its own, which is the first branch any analysis of this failure has to take, and it needs no core dump, no rebuilt wheel and no reproduction. Enabling accelerator telemetry on the hero gang is the cheapest single change that would improve the next occurrence.

## TL;DR

The final Hero forecast is 0.7406 Paloma BPB. Kimi K2 Base measures 0.6754 BPB, 8.8% lower than the forecast, and is lower on 14 of 16 subsets. Nemotron 3 Ultra has the lowest current-suite UncheatableEval result at 0.4663 BPB; Kimi is second at 0.4781 BPB.

![Hero and open-weight models by Paloma subset](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/hero-open-weight-ppl/2026.09.04.1/paloma-subset-forecasts.png)

## Description

Compare Hero with open-weight base models on the same evaluation data. Report bits per byte (BPB) because token perplexity is not comparable across tokenizers.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Measure each base model with the Hero evaluation protocol. Add each result to the same comparison.

## Status

### Paloma

| Model | BPB |
|---|---:|
| Kimi K2 Base | 0.6754 |
| Hero final forecast | 0.7406 |

| Hero with token dropping, step 45,837 | 0.8868 |

### Current 15-subset UncheatableEval

| Model | BPB |
|---|---:|
| Nemotron 3 Ultra-550B-A55B-Base | 0.4663 |

| Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base | 0.5245 |
| Hero without token dropping, step 45,837 | 0.5362 |
| Hero with token dropping, step 45,837 | 0.6220 |

The 7-subset and 15-subset UncheatableEval values are not directly comparable.

Each subset forecast fits BPB as a function of Paloma macro loss across 77 paired ladder measurements. It then applies the preregistered macro-loss scaling law. Fifteen fits have `R² ≥ 0.997`; Twitter AAE has `R² = 0.971`.

The FLOP axis uses `6 × active parameters × training tokens` estimates. Nano is at `5.25e23` FLOPs. Qwen is at `6.48e23` FLOPs, assuming 3B active parameters and 36T tokens. OLMo is at `1.06e24` FLOPs from 32B parameters and 5.50T tokens. Trinity is at about `1.33e24` FLOPs, assuming 13B active parameters and 17T tokens. Super is at least `1.8e24` FLOPs because NVIDIA reports more than 25T training tokens. Seed is at `2.59e24` FLOPs from 36B parameters and 12T tokens. Kimi is at about `2.98e24` FLOPs, using 32B active parameters and 15.5T tokens. Ultra is at about `6.6e24` FLOPs, assuming 55B active parameters and about 20T tokens. Gemma's training token count is unknown, so plots show it as a dashed reference line. Exact FLOPs for the hybrid MoE models are unknown.

A bootstrap over the four ladder runs gives 0.7404–0.7432 macro BPB. This range covers the loss-to-BPB conversion, not error in the loss forecast.

The forecast assumes a 4K context, the original data mix, and the planned token count. These inputs can change before training ends. Training-data overlap with the evaluation sets is unknown. We do not have a final UncheatableEval forecast.

- 2026-08-31: Limit the final forecast to Paloma. UncheatableEval has no final forecast.
